newsitem.title: USA: Cargo plane crashes in Miami, 4 crew presumed dead.
newsitem.headline: Cargo plane crashes in Miami, 4 crew presumed dead.

text.p: A Fine Air cargo jet crashed seconds after takeoff from Miami International Airport on Thursday, scattering flaming wreckage through a busy commercial district and apparently killing four crew members.

The DC-8-61F crashed before dozens of horrified witnesses who said it appeared to wobble in the air before plummeting to the ground, skidding across a six-lane road and crashing into the parking lot of a shopping mall at lunchtime.
The flaming wreckage set fire to cars, trucks and parts of buildings, sending orange fireballs and dense clouds of black smoke into the air.
Authorities said four crew members, a pilot, co-pilot, engineer and security guard were presumed dead, though only three bodies had been found.
Officials and witnesses said it was miraculous no one on the ground had been killed. At least two people were injured.
"This was a tragic crash, a terrible incident," Dade County Mayor Alex Penelas said at the scene. But "we indeed were very, very lucky. This could have been a much worse incident."
It was the first crash of a jetliner in south Florida since the May 1996 crash of a Valujet DC-9, which plunged into the Everglades, killing all 110 people on board.
Fine Air Flight 101, carrying 80,000 lbs (36,300 kg) of clothing material, took off in clear weather headed to Santo Domingo, Dominican Republic.
Witnesses said one of the plane's engines appeared to catch fire seconds after takeoff, sending the jet into a nosedive just off the end of a runway.
"It dropped like a rock -- boom -- right out of the sky," witness George Foch said. "It was incredible. It just dropped."

The plane disintegrated when it plunged into a busy commercial area of warehouses, offices and shops on the western edge of the Miami airfield, narrowly missing cars and pedestrians as it skidded, witnesses said.

"I looked to my left and this plane's coming at me," said a witness, adding the jet missed her by about 30 feet (nine metres). "I'm still shaking. It happened right in from of me. All I could think of was 'I've got to get out of here'."
Television images showed a blackened swath across busy Milam Dairy Road where it appeared the plane had skidded before coming to a halt in the parking lot.

The flaming wreckage crushed cars, scorched pavement, singed palm trees and knocked down fences. A towering column of black smoke was visible from downtown Miami, more than 10 miles (16 km) away. Firefighters blanketed the crash site in white retardant foam to smother flames.

Police and pickets from a UPS facility nearby scrambled to the scene. Bill Garcia, who was on the picket line, echoed other witnesses who said one of the plane's engines appeared to have caught fire in the air.
"All of a sudden it veered to the right, then to the left, we could see an engine on fire, then it nosedived," he said. "It looked like a missile."

National Transportation Safety Board investigators at the scene said there had been no emergency transmission from the pilot. Both the flight data recorder and cockpit voice recorder had been recovered.
Fine Air Services Inc mainly delivers cargo to Latin America and the Caribbean. Its initial public offering of stock hit the NASDAQ exchange on Wednesday.

The carrier is one of the largest international cargo operators at Miami's airport, a hub for Latin American trade. Cargo represents about 58 percent of Fine's business. It also does aircraft maintenance.

Nancy Aders, Fine Air vice president of sales, said the crash was the first for the 7-year-old airline. "We just went through an extensive FAA inspection and passed with flying colours three weeks ago," she told Fox News.
The plane was originally delivered to now-defunct Eastern Airlines in 1968 and became part of the Fine Air fleet in July 1993.
